idiom_name: RAII MutexGuard from Mutex::lock() (dropped at scope end)
implementation_notes: std::sync::Mutex owns the data it protects and hands it out only through a MutexGuard, whose Drop releases the mutex, so the scope-bound release is enforced by ownership and cannot be forgotten. lock() returns a Result because a panic in another thread poisons the mutex; the guard can be dropped explicitly to end the critical section early. In async code a std guard cannot be held across .await (MutexGuard is not Send), so tokio::sync::Mutex (Send guard, FIFO) is the async counterpart, and parking_lot::Mutex is the faster no-poisoning alternative with the same guard shape.
pitfalls: Holding a std guard across .await does not compile for Send futures; use tokio::sync::Mutex or end the critical section before awaiting to avoid blocking the runtime.
Poisoning: a panic while holding the lock makes later lock().unwrap() panic too - decide deliberately between unwrap, poison().into_inner(), or parking_lot's non-poisoning mutex.
A temporary such as `map.lock().unwrap().insert(..)` releases the guard at the end of the statement, so a multi-statement critical section silently loses protection.
The guard borrows the mutex, so it cannot be returned or stored in a longer-lived structure without extending the critical section; explicit drop() makes the end of the scope visible.
Mutex is not reentrant: locking the same mutex twice in one thread deadlocks (std) or panics (some alternative implementations).
